strengths: The core idea—grounding hand-designed PDDL abstractions in a new domain by using an LLM to synthesize a Python transition model, then planning bilevel-ly with Fast Downward + BFS—is a sensible and clearly articulated instantiation of TBRL that addresses two real limitations of prior work (restrictive theory languages like VGDL, and slow simulators).

The iterative refinement loop (compare predicted vs. actual transitions, use abstract-plan labels to focus LLM refinement, enumerate precondition-feasible exploratory subplans) is well motivated and illustrated with worked examples (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 9).

The evaluation spans several qualitatively different domains (Sokoban, Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, KekeCompetition/Baba is You) and includes an ablation of the bilevel abstractions (Table 3) showing large planning-time gains, plus a transfer experiment (KekeCompetition world model applied to Baba is AI) that is genuinely interesting.

The limitations section is honest: it explicitly acknowledges that hand-engineering abstractions is a major scalability hurdle and identifies learning abstractions, stochastic/continuous domains, and larger worlds as open problems.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is thin for the strength of the claims. Each domain has very few levels (5, 4, 13, 17), results appear to be from single runs with no seeds, error bars, or variance reporting (Table 3 says 'averaged over 5 runs' for runtimes only), and 'progress %' in Fig. 11 is never precisely defined. Success/API-call tables are essentially case studies, not statistically meaningful comparisons.

The most relevant baseline is missing: WorldCoder (Tang et al., 2024), which also synthesizes Python world models via LLM without abstractions, is discussed in related work as closely related but is never compared against. The 'ablated' condition in Table 3 removes abstractions but does not substitute an LLM-only world-model approach, so Question 2 ('do explicit code-based world models beat implicit ones?') is only answered against GPT-o1 plan generation, not against the closest method.

The central 'learning' claim is confounded by heavy hand-crafting. The PDDL domains embed substantial domain-specific knowledge (e.g., boxes_stuck, rule_formable, move_between_bottleneck with region structure), and the Python predicate/checker bridge functions are also supplied. The paper frames this as mirroring human prior knowledge, but there is no human data or cognitive-science evaluation despite the framing, so significance for the human-learning narrative is unsupported; as an ML systems contribution the hand-designed abstractions substantially limit generality.

The EMPA comparison (Question 4) is promised in Section 4 but never actually reported: no table compares TheoryCoder's API usage or success on Sokoban/Push Boulders 1 with EMPA's numbers; the claim that it 'solved VGDL tasks where EMPA previously struggled' rests on citing EMPA's failures rather than a head-to-head experiment.

Reproducibility is weak: the code link in footnote 1 is a placeholder ('https://github.com' with no repository path), the 'domain's natural language description' given in prompts (a potentially crucial input) is only gestured at, and details such as how the checker functions are written/validated and how BFS termination and cost of simulation failures are handled are unspecified. Typos and inconsistencies ('exceute', 'KekeCompetiton', a reference to 'Fig. 3' that should be Table 3, undefined reward r in Eq. 1) suggest insufficient polish.

The GPT-o1 baseline comparison is somewhat apples-to-oranges (different model for TheoryCoder vs. baseline); while the justification for GPT-o1 is given, there is no ablation using the same underlying LLM for both approaches, and no analysis of how sensitive TheoryCoder's success is to the particular LLM (temperature 0.7, single model).

strengths: The core idea is appealing: combining LLM-based program synthesis of Python transition models with PDDL-based bilevel planning is a sensible instantiation of theory-based RL, and the system is clearly explained with helpful figures (Figs. 1-3) and a concrete worked example of world-model revision (Fig. 9).
The paper is honest about its main limitation: the PDDL abstractions are hand-designed, and the limitations section explicitly flags this as the central open problem rather than hiding it.

The transfer experiment (world model learned on KekeCompetition solving Baba is AI levels without further learning) and the ablation of bilevel vs. flat planning (Table 3, showing timeouts ablated) are the most informative results, and support the claim that structured code world models are reusable and that abstractions speed up planning.
The exploratory-plan mechanism for refining the world model (Algorithm 1, Figs. 4-5) is a reasonable and interesting design for targeted model revision.
weaknesses: The central 'learning' claim is much narrower than the framing suggests. The PDDL domain files, problem files, checker functions, and natural-language domain descriptions are all hand-coded per domain, and the paper admits the low-level transition function is the *only* learned component. The claim of generalizing 'quickly to new problem domains' therefore rests on hard-coded transferable knowledge, which substantially undercuts the headline contribution and the cognitive-science framing.

The evaluation is very small and lacks statistical rigor: 4-17 levels per domain, single runs for the API-call tables (no seeds/variance reported for Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), and success rates of 100% for TheoryCoder leave little signal to analyze. Conclusions are drawn from a handful of levels.

The main baseline comparison is not apples-to-apples: TheoryCoder uses GPT-4o while the LLM-only baseline uses GPT-o1 (a different, stronger reasoning model). The authors justify this, but it makes the '24.5x reduction in API usage' claim hard to interpret, and there is no comparison against a GPT-4o LLM-only agent or against closely related systems such as WorldCoder (Tang et al., 2024), which the paper itself identifies as the nearest prior work.

API calls are used as a proxy for 'sample efficiency,' but they are a poor proxy: an API call is a cost metric, not an environment-interaction metric, and the number of environment steps executed by each method is not reported. BFS over the learned world model can consume arbitrarily many simulated steps.

Domain knowledge leaks into the prompts: both the baseline and TheoryCoder receive natural-language descriptions of the domain, and the world-model prompts contain substantial hints (e.g., 'YOU MUST ATTEMPT TO MODEL ALL THE MECHANICS FROM THE ACTION SPACE', advice on using .endswith to generalize). It is unclear how much of the success comes from these carefully engineered prompts rather than the architecture.

The 'checker' functions that bridge PDDL effects to low-level states are also hand-designed per domain (Section 3.3.2), but this is not clearly acknowledged as an additional hand-crafted component; the difficulty of designing these is a hidden cost of the approach.

Presentation issues: large amounts of whitespace on several pages (pp. 1, 7, 10, 12-13), incomplete code URL (footnote 1 reads 'https://github.com .' with no actual repository), and figures with awkward layout reduce polish and reproducibility.

The transfer result is less impressive than claimed: KekeCompetition and Baba is AI are two open-source implementations of essentially the same game, so transfer across them is expected for a correct Python world model and does not strongly evidence compositional generalization.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and cleanly executed: grounding hand-coded PDDL abstractions in a domain by using an LLM to synthesize a Python transition model, then exploiting that hierarchy with a bilevel planner (Fast Downward + BFS). This is a sensible and mostly novel combination of program-synthesis world models (e.g., WorldCoder, Dainese et al.) with abstract bilevel planning, and the paper positions it well against TBRL/EMPA, LLM-planning, and bilevel-planning literatures.

The empirical results support the central claims within their scope: TheoryCoder uses dramatically fewer LLM API calls than a GPT-o1 planning baseline (e.g., 2 vs 49 on BabyAI, 1 vs 25 on Sokoban), solves levels GPT-o1 fails on, and achieves substantial planning speedups from abstractions (Table 3), including timeouts avoided via the push_to_hole and move_between_bottleneck abstractions.

The transfer result (Section 4.6) is a genuinely compelling demonstration: the world model synthesized for KekeCompetition solves all 40 Baba is AI levels without additional learning, supporting the compositionality claim for code-based world models.

The paper is generally well written, with good illustrative figures (Figs. 2-5, 9) that walk through the initialization, refinement, and exploration loop concretely, and example prompts in the appendix that aid reproducibility of the LLM interactions.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: it clearly identifies the hand-designed abstractions as the central scalability bottleneck and proposes plausible future directions (LLM-generated PDDL domains, continuous/stochastic domains).
weaknesses: The evaluation is small and statistically fragile. There are only four domains with roughly 4-17 levels each, results appear to be from single runs (no seeds, error bars, or variance over LLM stochasticity despite temperature 0.7), and runtime ablations are averaged over only 5 runs. With GPT-4o-based synthesis, run-to-run variance could be large, and the reported success rates and API-call counts may not be robust.

The degree of prior knowledge embedded in the system weakens the 'learning' claim. The PDDL abstractions are hand-designed per domain and encode substantial task structure (e.g., the Sokoban push_to_hole operator with the boxes_stuck predicate, and the KekeCompetition rule_formed/rule_formable predicates essentially give away the rule-formation mechanics). Combined with natural-language domain descriptions in the prompts and the fact that these games are likely in GPT-4o's training data, it is hard to disentangle learned world modeling from retrieval of known game mechanics. No ablation isolates the contribution of the abstraction design versus the LLM's prior knowledge.

The baseline comparison is not fully fair and lacks key baselines. The most obvious comparator, WorldCoder (Tang et al., 2024), which the paper itself identifies as closest related work (LLM-synthesized Python world models), is not compared against, even though it would isolate the value of the bilevel/abstraction component. The GPT-o1 baseline also differs in role (direct planner vs. model refiner), and TheoryCoder receives the domain description and abstraction files, making API-call-count comparisons hard to interpret.

There are presentation and technical-consistency issues: Algorithm 1 line 10 executes actions with T-hat (the learned model) rather than the environment, which appears to be an error or at least confusing; the code availability footnote is incomplete ('https://github.com .'); PDDL 1.2 is cited while features shown (typed parameters) go beyond it; and some claims (e.g., 'up to 24.5x reduction in API usage') are computed from very few levels.

The exploration mechanism is heuristic and its coverage is not analyzed. Exploratory plans are enumerated from satisfiable preconditions of the hand-coded operators, so failure modes when the abstraction set or precondition encoding is wrong are unexplored; the Level 11 walkthrough shows the refinement loop can waste several API calls on irrelevant edits, but there is no systematic characterization of when refinement converges or fails.

Scope is limited to small, deterministic, fully observable 2D grid worlds with text-based state representations; the claimed relevance to human-like sample efficiency and to TBRL as a cognitive model is asserted but no human comparison or cognitive-science evaluation is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses two concrete and well-motivated limitations of prior theory-based RL (EMPA): restrictive theory languages (VGDL) and unscalable planning. Replacing VGDL with LLM-synthesized Python transition models and adding PDDL-based bilevel planning (Fast Downward + BFS) is a sensible and clearly articulated architecture.

Evaluation spans four distinct domains (Sokoban, Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, KekeCompetition/Baba is You), including the conceptually challenging Baba is You which previous program-synthesis and LLM-only approaches struggle with, and reports multiple relevant metrics (API calls, success rate, steps, planning runtime, tokens).

The ablation in Table 4 isolating the value of bilevel abstractions is convincing for the computational-efficiency claim (e.g., Sokoban level 4: 0.40s vs. 149.70s; Push Boulders level 3: 434.89s vs. TIMEOUT), and comparisons to WorldCoder and EMPA give useful external reference points.

The paper is commendably transparent about failure modes (Section 4.7: overgeneralized rules like 'goop causes death' blocking solutions), includes a training-data-contamination check with a newly designed game (Section 4.8), and has an honest limitations discussion acknowledging that hand-designed abstractions are a major scalability bottleneck.

The revision mechanism, where replay buffers are labeled by abstract subplans to give the LLM high-level semantic clues about which part of the code to fix (Fig. 2, Fig. 10), is a neat and well-illustrated idea.
weaknesses: The central 'learning' claim is substantially confounded. The PDDL domain/problem files are hand-coded per domain, and the LLM synthesis prompt includes a natural-language description of the domain (Section 4.1; Appendix A does not actually show this description's content). Given that domain descriptions, hand-designed operators/predicates, and even Python predicate stubs ('from predicates import *') are provided, it is unclear how much of the reported success comes from learned theory inference versus injected prior knowledge. This directly undercuts the framing that the agent 'learns a low-level transition model from observations' in a way comparable to TBRL/EMPA or human theory learning.

The baseline comparison is weak and possibly unfair. The only main baseline is a GPT-o1 LLM-only agent; there is no comparison against, e.g., WorldCoder's full method on the same domains, MCTS with the learned model, AutumnSynth, or an LLM agent given the same state text and plan-revision feedback in a stronger scaffold. The claim that TheoryCoder outperforms 'approaches based on directly synthesizing a policy' rests on a single, narrowly implemented baseline with an asymmetric setup (GPT-4o + planning vs. GPT-o1 raw).

Evaluation rigor is limited: results appear to be single runs per level at temperature 0.7 with a closed-source model (no seeds/variance reported except Table 4's 5-run runtime average); domains contain only 4-17 levels of small deterministic grid worlds. The abstract's claim of 'diverse and challenging grid-world games' oversells; there is no evidence the approach scales beyond these carefully curated benchmarks, and the authors' own out-of-distribution tests (Section 4.7) show failure after 25 API calls.

API-call count is a weak proxy for sample efficiency and flatters TheoryCoder: a learned world model reused across levels yields 0 additional 'calls,' but the baseline's effective compute is compared on an incommensurate axis. Also, Table 3's 'Steps Taken' for GPT-o1 (9 vs. 197) is misleading since GPT-o1 fails most levels and thus takes fewer steps; Figure 6 shows GPT-o1's learning efficiency on Sokoban is close to TheoryCoder's (0.022 vs. 0.025), which sits oddly with the text's claim that TheoryCoder's efficiency is 'far greater.'

The formal presentation is thin relative to the claims. Equations (1)-(4) merely restate that predicted and actual transition sets are shown to an LLM; Algorithm 1 contains an unstructured 'goto' and informal re-execution semantics; there is no analysis of when the refinement loop converges, what happens with stochastic dynamics, or guarantees on the synthesized model. The paper is essentially an empirical systems contribution without theoretical grounding.

Reproducibility concerns: the method depends on closed-source API behavior (GPT-4o/GPT-o1), the crucial natural-language domain descriptions are referenced but not shown, and no code release is mentioned. Reproducing the exact results would likely be impossible once model versions change.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and interesting problem: scaling theory-based RL beyond restrictive DSLs like VGDL by using LLM-synthesized Python world models combined with bilevel (PDDL + BFS) planning. The overall system design is coherent and clearly illustrated (Figs. 1-5, Algorithm 1).

Evaluation spans multiple domains (Sokoban, Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, KekeCompetition/Baba is You), including domains not expressible in VGDL, and compares against both an LLM-only planner (GPT-o1) and prior TBRL (EMPA) and program-synthesis (WorldCoder) agents.

The ablation on bilevel planning (Table 4) is informative, showing substantial runtime gains from hierarchical abstractions on the larger VGDL state spaces (e.g., hours reduced to minutes; timeouts avoided).

The paper is unusually candid about limitations: Section 4.7 provides a genuine failure analysis (world model overgeneralization on levels requiring character sacrifice), Section 4.8 tests a custom game to probe training-data contamination, and the conclusion honestly acknowledges that abstractions are hand-designed.
The use of abstract-plan-labeled replay buffers to guide LLM world-model refinement (Fig. 10) is a sensible and potentially reusable idea.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution - that hierarchical abstractions benefit learning and planning - is significantly undermined by the fact that the PDDL abstractions are entirely hand-designed per domain and the domain/problem files are hard-coded (Sec. 3.3.1). Section 4.4 essentially shows that success hinges on carefully engineered predicates (e.g., boxes_stuck, move_between_bottlenecks, not_near_door) tailored to each environment, which limits generality and creates a major confound: it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the LLM-synthesized world model versus expert-designed abstractions.

The evaluation is small-scale and statistically weak: 4-17 levels per game, single runs with no variance reported for most experiments (only Table 4 averages over 5 runs), and non-deterministic LLM calls (temperature 0.7) with no error bars. Success rates and API-call counts could easily fluctuate across seeds; no significance analysis is provided.

The baseline comparison is arguably unfair: TheoryCoder uses GPT-4o while the LLM-only baseline uses the (more expensive) GPT-o1; the retry structures and feedback given to each method differ; and the 'steps taken' comparison with EMPA (Table 3) uses a 500-step budget not fully described. The WorldCoder comparison is confined to one domain with token-count as the primary metric.

The 'sample efficiency' claim is largely a claim about API-call counts, which is a gameable and narrow proxy: TheoryCoder reuses a learned world model and does 0 API calls on later levels, but the underlying BFS planning cost can be very large (e.g., 434.89s in Table 4, level 1 at 58.38s). The paper concedes this only speculatively rather than quantifying total compute across methods.

Formal content is thin: the mathematical framing in Sec. 3 (Eqs. 1-4) restates the prompting pipeline without providing any guarantees or analysis (e.g., on convergence, soundness of refinement, or when exploration will discover missing dynamics). Algorithm 1 has no termination or correctness properties.

Several technical details are underspecified or inconsistent: the exploration mechanism (Section 3.2 is referenced but the content appears under 3.3.1), how exploratory plans are enumerated and bounded, how the 'checker' predicates are obtained for each domain, and how robustness is affected by prompt engineering (Sec. 4.7 admits ad-hoc syntax instructions were added to improve robustness).
Reproducibility concerns: the method depends on closed-source LLM APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-o1), and no code or prompts-per-domain release is stated, making independent replication difficult.

Novelty is moderate: the paper primarily combines existing ingredients (LLM code world models as in WorldCoder/Tang et al. 2024, bilevel PDDL planning as in task-and-motion-planning literature, TBRL as in Tsividis et al. 2021). The most novel element - abstract-plan-guided refinement - is not studied in depth (e.g., no controlled comparison isolating it from abstraction design).

The claim that solved VGDL tasks 'where EMPA previously struggled' rests on only two games (Sokoban, Push Boulders 1), and the learning-efficiency comparison in Fig. 6 lacks detail on how EMPA was re-run or whether its original published numbers were used under comparable budgets.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: the paper identifies two concrete limitations of prior TBRL systems (restrictive theory languages like VGDL, and non-scalable value-based planning) and addresses each with a specific mechanism (LLM-synthesized Python transition models; bilevel planning with PDDL abstractions and Fast Downward + BFS).

The system is coherent and the iterative loop (high-level planning, low-level grounding, error-driven refinement, exploratory plans) is well illustrated through Figures 1-5 and Algorithm 1, making the method easy to follow and in principle reproducible in design.

Empirically strong headline results: large reductions in API calls vs. a GPT-o1 LLM-only baseline across four domains (e.g., 1-7 calls vs. 19-49), better success rates than EMPA on Sokoban and Push Boulders 1, and substantially lower token cost than WorldCoder (Table 7).

Useful ablation: Table 4 quantifies the runtime benefit of bilevel planning (e.g., 24.58s vs. TIMEOUT on Sokoban level 5), directly supporting the claim that hierarchical abstractions improve planning efficiency, and Section 4.4 gives concrete examples of why specific predicates/operators matter.

Good scientific hygiene in places: a failure-mode analysis (Section 4.7) identifying overgeneralization in the world model, a contamination check with a custom game not in GPT-4o's training data (Section 4.8), and an honest limitations section acknowledging that abstractions are hand-engineered.
weaknesses: The central 'learning' component is narrow: only the low-level Python transition model is learned; the PDDL domain and problem files (the abstractions that the paper argues are the key enabler) are hand-designed per domain. This significantly limits the scalability and generality claims, and the paper is transparent about this, but it means the contribution is more of an engineering integration than a general learning method.

Evaluation rigor is limited: results appear to come from small numbers of levels (4-17 per domain) with no error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance reported, despite acknowledged run-to-run variability in Section 4.7 (the agent sometimes gets stuck early and requires a restart). How many restarts/seeds underlie Tables 1-8 is unclear.

Baseline comparisons have confounds: TheoryCoder uses GPT-4o while the LLM-only baseline uses the (different and more powerful) GPT-o1; the choice is justified but makes the comparison non-categorical. The 'heavy' prompting baseline for Keke is a partial mitigation, but a GPT-4o LLM-only baseline and/or TheoryCoder-with-GPT-o1 condition would strengthen the claims.

The comparison to EMPA is somewhat unfair in framing: EMPA learned theories from a restricted grammar via inference, whereas TheoryCoder inherits the massive prior of a pretrained LLM (essentially the entire Python-speaking internet), so 'solves games EMPA failed on' speaks more to the LLM prior than to TBRL methodology per se.

Novelty is moderate: the combination of LLM-based Python world model synthesis (WorldCoder, Tang et al. 2024), LLM-constructed PDDL models (Guan et al. 2023; Wong et al. 2024), and bilevel planning with classical planners (existing TAMP practice) are all established ingredients; the contribution is their composition plus the abstraction-anchored refinement scheme, which is valuable but incremental.

Presentation issues: several tables report metrics that are hard to interpret in isolation (e.g., Table 3 shows GPT-o1 taking 9 steps vs. TheoryCoder's 197, which is only meaningful with the success rates; Figure 6's learning-efficiency values are tiny and the metric definition makes cross-game comparison opaque). Minor typos ('exceute', 'knoweldge', 'effiency') and an informal 'goto' in Algorithm 1 suggest a need for another editing pass.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release or repository is mentioned, and results depend on specific prompts (Appendix A), closed-source model versions, and tuning choices (temperature 0.7, retry budgets), which would make exact replication difficult.
The formalism in Section 3.4 (Eqs. 1-4) is largely descriptive notation around an LLM prompt rather than an analysis with guarantees or quantitative characterization of when refinement converges.
